waypoints.name: Killen Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Reached on Forest Roads 23, 21 and 2329 from the Randle or Trout Lake side. FR-2329 holds snow well into early summer, so check the road before committing — parties blocked short of the trailhead have had to walk or bushwhack an extra mile or more of road and forest to reach it.

waypoints.name: High Camp Trail Junction
waypoints.directions: Follow Killen Creek Trail #113 up through subalpine forest and meadow for about three miles to the Pacific Crest Trail, and cross straight over onto the High Camp Trail. Killen Creek, crossed low on the trail, is the last dependable running water; everything above is melted snow. The tread thins out above treeline and is easy to lose in the dark or a whiteout, so note landmarks on the way up or carry a track.

waypoints.name: High Camp
waypoints.directions: Another mile on the High Camp Trail ends it at the edge of the Adams Glacier's lateral moraine. Sheltered bivy sites sit slightly higher, in a shallow snow gully just left of the moraine, and more camping is scattered across the benches above that.

waypoints.name: Adams Glacier Base
waypoints.directions: A patchy path runs past the upper camping area and up moraine and snow to the glacier toe, where parties rope up. Judge the timing generously — the volcano's scale flattens distance out and this leg routinely runs two hours. The point of the very early start is to be through the icefall before the sun starts working on it.

waypoints.name: Mount Adams Summit
waypoints.directions: The usual line takes the right-hand side of the glacier for roughly the first two-thirds, threading ice steps and serac lanes, then cuts back left high up onto the unbroken snow of the summit plateau. Which side of the upper icefall goes changes from year to year, and the left-hand option has been found far steeper than the grade suggests — sustained 55 to 65 degrees rather than moderate — so look at it in daylight from below before committing. The crossing beneath the ice cliffs is the stretch to move through fastest, on thin bridges and with backtracking common. Above the icefall the angle eases and two or three false summits stand between you and the true one, so keep navigating rather than trusting the first high point.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Nooksack River Bridge / FR 38 Gate
waypoints.note: Gated bridge on FR 38 (Dailey Quarry Road) off Mosquito Lake Road; park at the gate even if open; no parking permit is needed, but the private timberland road beyond requires the landowner's fee access permit, and many parties bike it.
waypoints.directions: From WA-542, turn onto Mosquito Lake Road and follow it to FR-38 (the Dailey Quarry Road), then take FR-38 to its end at the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, around 1,200 feet. Park at the gate even if you find it open — no permit is required to park here, though the road is closed to vehicles beyond this point and most parties continue from here by mountain bike.

waypoints.name: Dailey Prairie
waypoints.note: Old logging/quarry road passes this open prairie flat (a DNR Natural Area Preserve) before dropping into the basin between the Twin Sisters.
waypoints.directions: Ride or walk the old quarry and logging roads up from the gate. The grade is easy but the network branches repeatedly and the correct fork is rarely the obvious one, so follow a recorded track rather than instinct. Wrong turns here are the most common way to lose time on this route.

waypoints.name: Orsino Creek Crossing
waypoints.note: Last reliable water on the route; climbers' path crosses here and most parties stash bikes at this point before continuing on foot.
waypoints.directions: Past the prairie the roadbed drops into the basin between the two Sisters, taking a succession of left-hand forks as it goes. The road deteriorates until it is too rough or overgrown to ride, usually marked by a large culvert pipe where the timber road ends. Stash bikes in the trees and fill water at the crossing, because this is the last reliable source on the route.

waypoints.name: Orsino Creek Basin / Red Talus Slope
waypoints.note: Brushy old road fades to a boot path through timber then a red talus field opening into the upper basin below the West Ridge; talus often snow-covered into midsummer.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the narrow climbers' path on foot heading southeast. It is brushy and wet in places but followable; it drops slightly, crosses a forested section, and simply ends at a red talus slope that often holds snow into midsummer. From the talus traverse up and right (south), over a timbered rib and past the ruins of an old log cabin, into the upper basin.

waypoints.name: West Ridge Notch
waypoints.note: Gain the West Ridge crest here, roughly 1,800 ft below the summit; higher up, from a second notch about 400 ft below the summit, a traverse right (south) leads to easier Class 2-3 gullies instead of the ridge crest.
waypoints.directions: Climb out of the basin on steep dirt, scree and talus toward the obvious low notch in the ridge above. Sight the notch from the basin floor before starting up, and expect poor footing the whole way; this is the least pleasant stretch of the day.

waypoints.name: Dihedral in the upper cliff band
waypoints.note: Prominent dihedral in the cliffy band around 6,500 ft, below the false summit that parties often mistake for the true top; loose, abrasive dunite rock and a couple of low-5th-class moves here if staying on the ridge crest rather than dropping to the south-face gullies.
waypoints.directions: Follow the ridge up from the notch, roughly two hours of class 2-3 scrambling that moves on and off the crest. The right (south) side is generally solid and the left side is looser, and holding strictly to the crest is harder than dropping slightly south to bypass steps. The dunite is abrasive and holds friction unusually well, but it is hard on hands and rope. The ridge steepens into a cliffy band around 6,500 ft where the large dihedral sits.

waypoints.name: South Twin Sister
waypoints.note: Highest point in the Twin Sisters Range; two USGS benchmark caps and a summit register are on top, with Mount Baker visible 10 miles to the northeast.
waypoints.directions: The first high point above the dihedral is not the top and carries no cairn or register. Continue along the crest a short distance, on the order of fifty yards, crossing talus and any lingering snow to the next high point, which holds the survey markers and the register. In fog this last short stretch is where parties stop short and turn around believing they have summited.

waypoints.name: North Fork Entiat Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 5606; self-issue Northwest Forest Pass/day-use fee kiosk at the lot, day-use only with no camping at the TH itself.
waypoints.directions: From US 97A in Entiat, turn onto Entiat River Road (County Road 19) at the bridge and drive about 32 miles up the valley; it becomes FS Road 51 along the way. Turn onto FS Road 5606 and follow it about 3 miles to the road end. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and a free self-issued Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is available at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Fern Lake Trail (#1436) junction
waypoints.note: Trail #1437 tops a switchbacking climb away from the river here where the short Fern Lake spur splits off; stay on #1437 toward the Pyramid Mtn Trail rather than detouring to the lake.
waypoints.directions: Trail #1437 runs up the North Fork Entiat valley for about six miles, mostly gentle beside the river before switchbacks lift you away from it. The tread carries a reputation for blowdown, so budget time for it even when reports say it is clear.

waypoints.name: Pyramid Mountain Trail (#1433) junction camp
waypoints.note: Flat clearing where Trail #1437 meets the Pyramid Mtn Trail; a nearby log/plank crossing has been reported to flex badly in high water and is the usual base camp before heading off-trail toward Saska Pass.
waypoints.directions: Roughly two and a half miles on from the Fern Lake spur, staying on #1437. Fill water at the crossing here: the drainages between this junction and the pass are seasonal and are often dry.

waypoints.name: Saska Pass
waypoints.note: Gain the pass off-trail via a steep dry streambed and a loose scree headwall; it marks the crest between the Emerald Peak basin and the Snow Brushy Creek burn drainage leading to Pinnacle's north side.
waypoints.directions: Leave the tread before it starts traversing toward the pass and climb the drainage directly; the traverse sidehills across scree and is slower and more tiring than going straight up. The headwall above the bench is loose enough to be worth a helmet, and it is worse for anyone climbing below you.

waypoints.name: Snow Brushy Creek burn-zone crossing
waypoints.note: Descend roughly 1,500 ft off the pass into the 2006/2015-era burn; ash-covered slopes and heavy standing/fallen burnt snags erase the tread, so carry a GPS track rather than relying on cairns.
waypoints.directions: Head straight down the far side of the pass rather than hunting for tread, because none survives here. The burn is open enough that the descent goes quickly, but every foot of it has to be regained on the way home, and the far bank climbs steeply straight out of the creek.

waypoints.name: Basin below Pinnacle's summit block
waypoints.note: Exit the burn into open larch basins on the peak's north side, then climb loose scree to a bench that sets up the final class 2-3 ridge traverse to the summit.
waypoints.directions: A steep and unrelenting climb of around 1,900 feet out of the creek: poor scree low down where the burn ends, easing as the ground opens higher up. This leg and the reclimb of the pass afterwards are what make the day long, not any difficulty on the peak itself.

waypoints.name: Pinnacle Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit (8,400 ft), first climbed 1948 by Dwight Watson and Ken Fleming; the standard finish is class 3 scrambling up the south-slope talus, which doubles as the descent line.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest on from the bench, keeping to its west side where the scrambling stays easiest. The rock here is noticeably more solid than the scree below, but it is still a hands-on class 3 finish rather than a walk-up.

wa_magic_mountain_northwest_ridge.itinerary: Two days from a Kool-Aid Lake camp is the sensible plan. Day 1: drive, 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass, over the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, drop to Kool-Aid Lake and camp (about 8 miles, ~5 hours). Day 2: cross to the base of the northwest ridge, climb it and the northwest face to the summit, descend the South Ridge back to camp, pack up and hike out over Cache Col. Parties on the full Ptarmigan Traverse can slot this in as a half-day objective from the Kool-Aid Lake camp in place of the more common South Ridge scramble.

wa_magic_mountain_southwest_cirque.itinerary: Two days. Day 1: drive in, hike 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass, cross the Cache Glacier to Cache Col, descend 600 ft and camp at Kool-Aid Lake (about 8 miles, ~5 hours). Day 2: climb into the southwest cirque, take a gully to the summit ridge and the top (2-3 hours), descend the South Ridge to camp, then pack and exit over Cache Col. As with the South Ridge, this is most naturally done as a side objective from the first camp on the Ptarmigan Traverse; a car-to-car day is about 19 miles round trip.

wa_magic_mountain_west_ridge.itinerary: Two days from a Kool-Aid Lake camp. Day 1: drive in, hike 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass, cross the Cache Glacier to Cache Col, drop 600 ft and camp at Kool-Aid Lake (about 8 miles, ~5 hours). Day 2: cross to the pocket glacier below the west face early while the snow is firm, cross the schrund, climb the route in four pitches or so, scramble to the summit, descend the South Ridge to camp, then pack out over Cache Col. Three days is more comfortable and lets you add the South Ridge or the Southwest Cirque as a second day's objective from the same camp.
